analysis.one_liner: Raises taxes on guns and ammunition to fund police hiring and gun-violence research.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to five House committees in February 2018, it got no hearing, no vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would roughly double the federal excise tax on firearms to 20% and put a 50% tax on ammunition, while raising the license fees gun dealers pay and the transfer tax on certain restricted weapons. The money would fund community police hiring, violence-prevention programs, CDC research on gun violence, and school-climate grants. It exempts purchases by the U.S. military and federal agencies. The bill was introduced by Representative Danny Davis with 12 Democratic cosponsors and never received any committee action or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities with high gun violence, who would gain from funded police hiring, violence-intervention programs, and CDC research on what prevents gun deaths; schools serving low-income students, which would get grants for restorative justice and anti-violence programs; and law enforcement agencies, which would receive hiring grants.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal excise tax on guns from 10% to 20% and puts a 50% excise tax on shells and cartridges, with revenue directed to public-safety programs.

Allocates the new revenue as 35% for community policing officer-hiring grants, 35% for Project Safe Neighborhoods, 10% for CDC research on gun violence and its prevention, 10% for background-check record improvement, 5% for community violence-prevention research, and 5% for school grants to reduce exclusionary discipline and youth entry into the justice system.

Doubles the annual license tax on firearms manufacturers and importers to $2,000 and raises it from $500 to $1,000 for dealers, pawnbrokers, and small makers, with inflation adjustments so the fees do not erode.

Raises the tax on transfers of heavily restricted weapons like machine guns and silencers from $200 to $500, and reclassifies certain semiautomatic pistols chambered for rifle rounds as restricted weapons subject to that tax.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition buyers, who would pay higher prices as the new taxes pass through from manufacturers and dealers; the firearms industry, which would face doubled excise taxes and doubled or higher annual license fees; and federal agencies would be exempt, so the cost falls on civilian purchases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: The 50% ammunition tax would raise the price of every box of shells and cartridges, a recurring cost paid by hunters, sport shooters, and gun owners, including those who use firearms for self-defense or subsistence hunting, not only by people who misuse guns.
The tax applies to lawful retail sales, so its effect on illegal gun trafficking is indirect: it funds enforcement and prevention programs but does not itself block prohibited purchasers.

Some of the police-hiring money could go to placing more armed officers in schools; the bill tries to limit this by requiring training, protections, and monitoring so school resource officers improve school climate and reduce referrals to the juvenile justice system, but critics of school policing would not find that binding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: programs aimed at gun violence and youth intervention get substantial dedicated funding, while every gun and ammo purchase gets more expensive. A 50% tax on ammunition is a heavy, recurring burden on gun owners, and the benefits depend on how well the funded programs work rather than on the tax deterring misuse directly. The design does protect conservation funding from being raided and tries to guard against school-police misuse, which suggests a serious drafting effort, but the burden on ordinary gun owners is significant and would be the bill's biggest political and fairness problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees, including Ways and Means, and to two subcommittees, and then sat untouched until the 115th Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Representative Danny Davis of Illinois introduced the bill on February 27, 2018, with 12 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The Speaker referred it to five committees at once: Ways and Means, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Energy and Commerce.
In early March 2018 it was referred to the Health subcommittee of Ways and Means and the Federal Lands subcommittee of Natural Resources, the last recorded action of any kind.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and it expired on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers kept the existing 10% excise tax and their current license fees because the bill died without a vote; gun buyers paid no new taxes. Communities affected by gun violence received none of the proposed funding.

industries.note: The bill doubles their excise tax to 20% on guns, adds a 50% tax on ammunition, and doubles their annual federal license tax to $2,000. Because the industry's revenue depends on sales volume, any tax designed to discourage purchases and fund regulation runs against its interest.
A 50% excise tax on shells and cartridges is far above the current 11% and would hit the most frequently purchased product in the industry. Consumers would pay most of it in higher prices.
The annual occupational tax on dealers would double from $500 to $1,000, with inflation increases afterward. Small shops operating on thin margins would feel this as a fixed cost.

They would pay the ammunition tax every time they bought ammo, a recurring cost unrelated to any misuse of firearms. The bill explicitly protects their existing Pittman-Robertson conservation funding at current levels, directing only the new tax revenue to public-safety programs.
